Nice Weather: the product direction

Everything that decides what the product does, in one place. The sliders are the real calculation: the table below recounts ten years of hourly weather (2016 to 2025) at 31 places as you drag, the same way the map will. Your taste is the default. Reply with what you'd change; anything you don't mention, I take as agreed.

Where on earth is best all year round?

T-shirt weather

Cool hours count in the sun, hot hours in the shade, as you'd choose yourself. For scale: San Diego or Málaga at 1 pm in winter feels 22 °C in the sun; at 4 pm in July, Seville feels 35 °C in the shade and Austin 37 °C.

The walk home at 9 pm

San Diego at 9 pm feels about 12 °C in January and 25 °C in August. Below your setting, the day is Fair at best.

Humidity

Measured as dew point, which is what you feel as muggy; relative humidity changes with the temperature. Typical summer days: Seville 15 °C, San Diego and Málaga 18 °C, Austin 21 °C; Bangkok and Singapore 24 to 25 °C all year. Each degree past your setting costs a little more.

Rain

Rain between 10:00 and 9 pm. A third of your amount costs a fifth of the day; twice your amount costs most of it.

Wind

Wind already counts in how warm it feels. This is the nuisance on top: dust, sand, hair. Cape Town in January averages 25 km/h (the "Cape Doctor"); Rotterdam in January 17 km/h.

Each cell is the share of days that month that are nice or better. A grey figure after a year total is the change from your default taste.

At your taste, two kinds of place beat SoCal: subtropical islands with a sunny, sheltered south coast (south Tenerife, Gran Canaria, Honolulu) and high, dry cities in the tropics (Nairobi at 1,800 m, Guadalajara at 1,550 m), warm every afternoon and never muggy. These are 31 places I picked; the map ranks every square on land, including places nobody thought of.

What a nice day is

T-shirt-and-shorts weather from 10:00 until the walk home at 9 pm. Each hour counts if it feels warm enough in the sun and not too hot in the shade. Cold costs faster than heat: an hour 5 °C below your lower setting no longer counts; above your upper setting it takes 10 °C. Rain, humidity and wind take a share off the day. If the walk home is colder than your evening setting, the day is Fair at best. A day is Nice when most of it works.

The same score grades each forecast day: Awful, Poor, Fair, Nice, Beautiful or Perfect.

You asked whether an average wind of 30 km/h should make a day Fair. Not on its own: wind already lowers how warm it feels, which is where most of its cost lies. At your setting, 30 km/h costs a tenth of the day and 45 km/h half.

I tested a sixth setting, a minimum of sunshine, and left it out. It barely changes anything, because days warm enough for a t-shirt are almost always sunny: nice days at every test place have a median of 8 to 10 sunny hours out of 12.

Austin, where you just were

Austin gets 118 nice days a year at your taste, and you picked its best month. October: 69% of days nice, highs around 30 °C and still 24 °C at 9 pm, so t-shirt day and night. November drops to 38%: highs around 23 °C but 14 °C at 9 pm, so warm middays and a layer for the evening. March and April come close to October (55% and 66%).

June to August is too hot and too humid: 4 to 15% nice, still 33 °C at 9 pm, with a dew point of 21 °C. December to February (6 to 24%) has highs of 17 to 20 °C and cold evenings.

You expected Austin in November to beat Málaga for t-shirt time. It does, narrowly: 38% of November days against Málaga's 36%, and both need a layer by 9 pm (Málaga about 14 °C). Neither is shorts all day.

Why SoCal isn't nice all year

San Diego gets 219 nice days a year at your taste and Los Angeles 216. From June to October it is t-shirt weather nearly all day and 20 to 25 °C at 9 pm. Winter middays are fine too: San Diego at 1 pm in January feels 22 °C in the sun.

The evening is what stops them in winter. San Diego feels about 12 °C at 9 pm in January, so December to February has 8 nice days out of 90 at your setting (Los Angeles 6). Slide the walk home to "don't mind" and that becomes 38 (37). Rain on about one January day in ten does the rest. So SoCal's winter is sunny, mild middays with cool evenings, and the evening slider is the choice that decides how good it looks.

Bay Area microclimates

They are large, and today's data barely sees them. On an average July afternoon Half Moon Bay is 17 °C, downtown San Francisco 19 °C, San Jose 28 °C and Livermore 32 °C. Each weather square is about 25 km across, too coarse to see a fog belt a few kilometres wide, so the data reads the foggy coast about 5 °C too warm and the inland valleys up to 4 °C too cold.

"Real temperatures" reshapes each day's hourly temperatures to that day's measured high and low at the station, 2016 to 2025. Sun, wind, humidity and rain stay as the weather data has them.

The fix is a fine climate map built from weather stations: PRISM, at 800 m, for the US. Each pixel's temperature is shifted by how much warmer or cooler that spot runs than its weather square, month by month. That gets every place to within 17 nice days a year of the real temperatures, against errors of up to 100 days today. Outside the US the same correction uses WorldClim, at about 1 km, as Theo's site does; I haven't tested that yet. One gap remains: fog also hides the sun, which a temperature map can't see, so the foggy coast may still read a little too nice.

So the Bay Area tops out at about 150 nice days a year, inland, against San Diego's 219. San Francisco in the table above is today's uncorrected data; it really gets about 70.

How the map keeps up with the sliders

Under 0.2 s for any change, anywhere on the map. Every 100 km square keeps a small sample of real days. When a slider moves, your device's graphics chip recounts them and adds the fine detail for height and coast pixel by pixel, the way Theo's map does. Nothing waits on a server while you drag. Sites does the heavy work in advance: it builds the samples, and the map at your default taste in full detail, every day, so the first view is instant.

I checked that the small day summary this needs gives the same answer as the full hour-by-hour calculation: the same verdict on 99 to 100% of days at 19 places, never more than 3 nice days a year apart. This page runs exactly that recount. The timing for the whole world on a phone is the first thing I measure when building.

What I'm fixing anyway

  • Coasts. Today coastal towns read 2 to 4 °C too cold, because each square mixes sea, coast and mountain. Taking temperature from the nearest land and correcting for height cuts the error to under 1 °C against weather stations. Cape Town still reads about 3 °C too hot in summer; that gets fixed before it goes live.
  • Rain. The data counts too many wet days in dry places: Málaga in January reads wet on 26% of days, its weather station 16.5%. I'll test Theo's correction against stations and keep whatever matches them.
  • Forecast and climate agree. Both use the same sun measure (from solar radiation) and the forecast adds gusts. 15 forecast days, as ECMWF gives; ECMWF's 9 km forecast when it becomes free.
  • The 20-year climate is built on Sites. It works; run one area at a time, the world would take weeks, so it runs in parallel.

At "t-shirt", even south Tenerife's winter mostly fails; at "don't mind", a cold evening never counts against a day.
